claim: Blood development in multicellular organisms relies on specific tissue microenvironments that nurture hematopoietic precursors and promote their self-renewal, proliferation, and differentiation.
source: Blood development in multicellular organisms relies on specific tissue microenvironments that nurture hematopoietic precursors and promote their self-renewal, proliferation, and differentiation.
evidence: This is a general statement about blood development that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field of hematopoiesis.

claim: The mechanisms driving blood cell homing and their interactions with hematopoietic microenvironments remain poorly understood.
source: The mechanisms driving blood cell homing and their interactions with hematopoietic microenvironments remain poorly understood.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current scientific understanding, representing the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Basement membrane composition plays a pivotal role in the formation of hematopoietic compartments in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Here, we use the Drosophila melanogaster model to reveal a pivotal role for basement membrane composition in the formation of hematopoietic compartments.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: By modulating extracellular matrix components, fly blood cells (hemocytes) can be relocated to tissue surfaces where they function similarly to their natural hematopoietic environment.
source: We demonstrate that by modulating extracellular matrix components, the fly blood cells known as hemocytes can be relocated to tissue surfaces where they function similarly to their natural hematopoietic environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing hemocyte relocation and function upon ECM manipulation.

claim: The Collagen XV/XVIII ortholog Multiplexin in tissue-basement membranes and the phagocytosis receptor Eater on hemocytes physically interact.
source: We establish that the Collagen XV/XVIII ortholog Multiplexin in the tissue-basement membranes and the phagocytosis receptor Eater on the hemocytes physically interact and are necessary and sufficient to induce immune cell-tissue association.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Multiplexin and Eater are necessary and sufficient to induce immune cell-tissue association.
source: We establish that the Collagen XV/XVIII ortholog Multiplexin in the tissue-basement membranes and the phagocytosis receptor Eater on the hemocytes physically interact and are necessary and sufficient to induce immune cell-tissue association.
evidence: This claim is supported by loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The cooperation of Multiplexin and Eater is an integral part of a homing mechanism that specifies and maintains hematopoietic sites in Drosophila.
source: These results highlight the cooperation of Multiplexin and Eater as an integral part of a homing mechanism that specifies and maintains hematopoietic sites in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: During mammalian embryonic development, hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) relocate to the fetal liver where they considerably expand in number before populating the spleen and bone marrow in late embryonic stages.
source: During mammalian embryonic development, the hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) relocate to the fetal liver where they considerably expand in number, before they populate the spleen and the bone marrow in late embryonic stages (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2018.

claim: Postnatally, transplanted HSCs primarily seed the hematopoietic niches within the bone marrow by recognizing specific signals on endothelial cells of blood vessels and undergoing trans-endothelial migration.
source: Postnatally, transplanted HSCs primarily seed the hematopoietic niches within the bone marrow by recognizing specific signals on the endothelial cells of the blood vessels, and undergoing trans-endothelial migration (Birbrair and Frenette, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Birbrair and Frenette, 2016.

claim: In the bone marrow, HSCs attach to endosteal cells, which together form the endosteal HSC niche capable of renewing the entire blood cell pool throughout life.
source: In the bone marrow, the HSCs attach to endosteal cells, which together form the endosteal HSC niche capable of renewing the entire blood cell pool throughout life (Birbrair and Frenette, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Birbrair and Frenette, 2016.

claim: The extracellular matrix (ECM) has been recognized as an essential component of hematopoietic stem cell niches.
source: Apart from various non-hematopoietic cells which guard HSC behavior, the extracellular matrix (ECM) has been recognized as an essential component of hematopoietic stem cell niches (Klamer and Voermans, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klamer and Voermans, 2014.

claim: The ECM provides a structured microenvironment to the niche and connects to HSCs through integrin-mediated adhesion.
source: The ECM provides a structured microenvironment to the niche and connects to HSCs through integrin-mediated adhesion (Gattazzo et al., 2014; Khurana et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gattazzo et al., 2014 and Khurana et al., 2016.

claim: Integrin-mediated mechanosensitive signals from the ECM regulate HSC proliferative capacity and differentiation.
source: In turn, this mechanosensitive signal feeds back on the stem cells to regulate their proliferative capacity or differentiation (Choi and Harley, 2012; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi and Harley, 2012 and Lee et al., 2013.

claim: The ECM is required for homeostatic maintenance of the HSC population.
source: Although mounting evidence points to the requirement for the ECM in the homeostatic maintenance of the HSC population (Klamer and Voermans, 2014), it remains unexplored if ECM alters the behavior of immune precursors solely by conveying mechanical signals or whether there are receptor-ligand interactions that depend on the recognition of specific ECM components which trigger activation of discrete signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klamer and Voermans, 2014.

claim: Drosophila immune cells (hemocytes) are present from early embryonic stages and reside in specific hematopoietic sites during development.
source: Similar to mammals, Drosophila immune cells, called hemocytes, are present from early embryonic stages, and reside in specific hematopoietic sites during development (Martinez-Agosto et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martinez-Agosto et al., 2007.

claim: In larval stages, hemocytes form three hematopoietic tissues: the circulation, the lymph gland, and the sessile hematopoietic pockets.
source: In the larval stages, hemocytes form three hematopoietic tissues: the circulation, the lymph gland and the sessile hematopoietic pockets (Honti et al., 2014; Letourneau et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Honti et al., 2014 and Letourneau et al., 2016.

claim: The circulation comprises mostly macrophage-like cells (plasmatocytes) and crystal cells, which participate in the melanization of encapsulated foreign objects.
source: The circulation comprises mostly macrophage-like cells (plasmatocytes) and crystal cells, which participate in the melanization of encapsulated foreign objects (e.g. parasitic wasp eggs) (Lanot et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lanot et al., 2001.

claim: Lamellocytes are a third type of hemocyte that are not present under homeostatic conditions but rapidly differentiate upon immune challenge.
source: These capsules are largely formed by a third type of hemocytes, the lamellocytes, which are not present under homeostatic conditions, but rapidly differentiate upon immune challenge (Lanot et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lanot et al., 2001.

claim: The lymph gland is a compact multi-lobe hematopoietic organ on the anterior end of the dorsal vessel where immune cell precursors differentiate into plasmatocytes and crystal cells.
source: Unlike the freely moving cells in the circulation, the lymph gland is a compact multi-lobe hematopoietic organ on the anterior end of the dorsal vessel, where immune cell precursors differentiate into plasmatocytes and crystal cells (Jung, 2005; Krzemien et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jung, 2005 and Krzemien et al., 2010.

claim: Lymph gland-derived hemocytes enter the circulation only during pupariation or upon immune challenge such as parasitic attack.
source: Importantly, the lymph gland-derived hemocytes enter the circulation only during pupariation or upon immune challenge such as parasitic attack (Krzemień et al., 2007; Sorrentino et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krzemień et al., 2007 and Sorrentino et al., 2002.

claim: Sessile hematopoietic pockets are located segmentally along the length of the larva in lateral and dorsal patches contained within epidermis and muscle tissue.
source: The sessile hematopoietic pockets are located segmentally along the length of the larva in lateral and dorsal patches contained within epidermis and muscle tissue (Makhijani et al., 2011; Márkus et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Makhijani et al., 2011 and Márkus et al., 2009.

claim: The sessile tissue is primarily composed of plasmatocytes, some of which undergo trans-differentiation into crystal cells.
source: The sessile tissue is primarily composed of plasmatocytes, some of which undergo trans-differentiation into crystal cells (Leitão and Sucena, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leitão and Sucena, 2015.

claim: The formation of sessile hematopoietic pockets is orchestrated by sensory neurons of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) that attract hemocytes and support their survival and proliferation in situ by secreting Activin-β.
source: It has been demonstrated that the formation of sessile hematopoietic pockets is orchestrated by sensory neurons of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) that not only attract hemocytes but also support their survival and proliferation in situ by secreting Activin-β, a ligand of the TGF-β family (Makhijani et al., 2017; Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Makhijani et al., 2017 and Makhijani et al., 2011.

claim: Plasmatocytes require cell-autonomous expression of Eater, a phagocytosis receptor of the Nimrod family, to maintain their attachment to sessile pockets.
source: Furthermore, plasmatocytes require the cell-autonomous expression of Eater, a phagocytosis receptor of the Nimrod family (Kocks et al., 2005), to maintain their attachment to sessile pockets (Bretscher et al., 2015; Melcarne et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kocks et al., 2005, Bretscher et al., 2015, and Melcarne et al., 2019.

claim: There is continuous exchange between circulating and sessile hemocytes.
source: While these mechanisms anchor the immune cells to the epidermis, they do not isolate them, as there is a continuous exchange between circulating and sessile hemocytes (Honti et al., 2010; Lanot et al., 2001; Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Honti et al., 2010, Lanot et al., 2001, and Makhijani et al., 2011.

claim: In response to stress insults, sessile hemocytes can be rapidly mobilized and enter circulation.
source: Moreover, in response to various stress insults sessile hemocytes can be rapidly mobilized and enter circulation (Márkus et al., 2009; Vanha-Aho et al., 2015), while reestablishing the stereotypical pattern of hematopoietic pockets when the challenge ceases (Makhijani et al., 2011), highlighting the dynamic nature of the sessile hematopoietic compartment as well as a requirement for homing cues and adhesive surfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Márkus et al., 2009 and Vanha-Aho et al., 2015.

claim: Sessile hemocytes reestablish the stereotypical pattern of hematopoietic pockets when stress challenges cease.
source: Moreover, in response to various stress insults sessile hemocytes can be rapidly mobilized and enter circulation (Márkus et al., 2009; Vanha-Aho et al., 2015), while reestablishing the stereotypical pattern of hematopoietic pockets when the challenge ceases (Makhijani et al., 2011), highlighting the dynamic nature of the sessile hematopoietic compartment as well as a requirement for homing cues and adhesive surfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Makhijani et al., 2011.

claim: Sessile hematopoietic pockets are formed in gaps between the larval epidermis and the body wall muscles.
source: Since the sessile hematopoietic pockets are formed in gaps between the larval epidermis and the body wall muscles (Makhijani et al., 2011), the immune cells are in intimate contact with the basement membranes covering these surfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Makhijani et al., 2011.

claim: Hemocytes can relocate to tissues with pathologically altered ECM composition and/or structure, such as imaginal discs or salivary glands with damaged basement membranes.
source: In fact, hemocytes can relocate to other tissues with pathologically altered ECM composition and/or structure, such as imaginal discs or salivary glands with damaged basement membranes (Casas-Tintó et al., 2015; Hauling et al., 2014; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008), tumors (Cordero et al., 2010; Kulshammer and Uhlirova, 2013; Pérez et al., 2017) or fibrotic adipose tissues (Zang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Casas-Tintó et al., 2015, Hauling et al., 2014, and Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008.

claim: Hemocytes can relocate to tumors.
source: In fact, hemocytes can relocate to other tissues with pathologically altered ECM composition and/or structure, such as imaginal discs or salivary glands with damaged basement membranes (Casas-Tintó et al., 2015; Hauling et al., 2014; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008), tumors (Cordero et al., 2010; Kulshammer and Uhlirova, 2013; Pérez et al., 2017) or fibrotic adipose tissues (Zang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cordero et al., 2010, Kulshammer and Uhlirova, 2013, and Pérez et al., 2017.

claim: Hemocytes can relocate to fibrotic adipose tissues.
source: In fact, hemocytes can relocate to other tissues with pathologically altered ECM composition and/or structure, such as imaginal discs or salivary glands with damaged basement membranes (Casas-Tintó et al., 2015; Hauling et al., 2014; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008), tumors (Cordero et al., 2010; Kulshammer and Uhlirova, 2013; Pérez et al., 2017) or fibrotic adipose tissues (Zang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zang et al., 2015.

claim: Hemocytes secrete ECM proteins such as Laminins and Collagen IV to cope with tissue insults and participate in developmental tissue remodeling.
source: As a mechanism to cope with such insults and to participate in developmental tissue remodeling, hemocytes secrete ECM proteins, such as Laminins or Collagen IV (Bunt et al., 2010; Töpfer et al., 2019), as well as ECM processing enzymes or assembly factors (Martinek et al., 2008; Nelson et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bunt et al., 2010 and Töpfer et al., 2019.

claim: Hemocytes secrete ECM processing enzymes and assembly factors.
source: As a mechanism to cope with such insults and to participate in developmental tissue remodeling, hemocytes secrete ECM proteins, such as Laminins or Collagen IV (Bunt et al., 2010; Töpfer et al., 2019), as well as ECM processing enzymes or assembly factors (Martinek et al., 2008; Nelson et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Martinek et al., 2008 and Nelson et al., 1994.

claim: Fat body-specific overexpression of Atf3 under the C7-GAL4 driver induced a lean phenotype and decreased lipid droplet size.
source: We have reported previously that the fat body-specific overexpression of Atf3 under the C7-GAL4 driver (Koyama and Mirth, 2016) (hereafter abbreviated as C7>Atf3WT) induced a lean phenotype and decreased lipid droplet size (Rynes et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rynes et al., 2012.

claim: C7>Atf3WT larvae show massive attachment of hemocytes to the adipose tissue surface.
source: Intriguingly, a closer examination of C7>Atf3WT larvae in which the fat body was visualized with a help of UAS-GFP and the hemocyte population with Hml:DsRed reporter (hereafter abbreviated as Hml:DsRed, C7>Atf3WT) revealed a massive attachment of hemocytes to the adipose tissue surface (Figure 1B, D and E), a phenotype not detected in control larvae (Figure 1A, C and E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, D, and E.

claim: Fat body-associated hemocytes (FBAHs) in Hml:DsRed, C7>Atf3WT larvae are densely packed and often form contiguous monolayers over the entire length of the adipose tissue.
source: The fat body-associated hemocytes (hereafter referred to as FBAHs) present in Hml:DsRed, C7>Atf3WT larvae were densely packed and often formed contiguous monolayers over the entire length of the adipose tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The characteristic pattern of sessile hematopoietic pockets is disrupted in Hml:DsRed, C7>Atf3WT larvae.
source: In contrast, the characteristic pattern of sessile hematopoietic pockets observed in controls was disrupted in Hml:DsRed, C7>Atf3WT larvae (Figure 1A and B), while the amount of circulating hemocytes was not significantly affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The amount of circulating hemocytes is not significantly affected in C7>Atf3WT larvae.
source: In contrast, the characteristic pattern of sessile hematopoietic pockets observed in controls was disrupted in Hml:DsRed, C7>Atf3WT larvae (Figure 1A and B), while the amount of circulating hemocytes was not significantly affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hemocytes associate with clones of Atf3 overexpressing adipocytes induced by the heat shock FLPout technique.
source: Importantly, we found that hemocytes also associated with clones of Atf3 overexpressing adipocytes induced by the heat shock FLPout (hsFLPout) technique (Figure 1F), suggesting that the attachment is an intrinsic property of the fat body cells with excessive Atf3 levels rather than a consequence of the systemic activation of blood cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Hemocyte attachment to Atf3 overexpressing fat body is an intrinsic property of the fat body cells rather than a consequence of systemic activation of blood cells.
source: Importantly, we found that hemocytes also associated with clones of Atf3 overexpressing adipocytes induced by the heat shock FLPout (hsFLPout) technique (Figure 1F), suggesting that the attachment is an intrinsic property of the fat body cells with excessive Atf3 levels rather than a consequence of the systemic activation of blood cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clonal experiment data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: No uptake of GFP-positive material originating from the fat body was observed in hemocytes on C7>Atf3WT fat bodies.
source: In support of this notion, neither the uptake of GFP-positive material originating from the fat body was observed in the hemocytes, nor signs of an encapsulation reaction, such as adhesion of lamellocytes or tissue melanization, were present in the case of C7>Atf3WT fat bodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No signs of encapsulation reaction, such as adhesion of lamellocytes or tissue melanization, are present on C7>Atf3WT fat bodies.
source: In support of this notion, neither the uptake of GFP-positive material originating from the fat body was observed in the hemocytes, nor signs of an encapsulation reaction, such as adhesion of lamellocytes or tissue melanization, were present in the case of C7>Atf3WT fat bodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and 1F.

claim: FBAHs project filopodia of varying lengths and lamellipodia, similar to sessile hemocytes.
source: Intriguingly, FBAHs, like sessile hemocytes (Lanot et al., 2001; Leitão and Sucena, 2015; Makhijani et al., 2011; Márkus et al., 2009), projected filopodia of varying lengths as well as lamellipodia (Figure 2A–B) and proliferated in situ as demonstrated by the Fly-FUCCI in vivo cell cycle reporter (Zielke et al., 2014) and immunostaining for a mitotic marker phospho-histone-H3 (pH3) (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and citations to previous studies.

claim: FBAHs proliferate in situ on the adipose tissue surface.
source: Intriguingly, FBAHs, like sessile hemocytes (Lanot et al., 2001; Leitão and Sucena, 2015; Makhijani et al., 2011; Márkus et al., 2009), projected filopodia of varying lengths as well as lamellipodia (Figure 2A–B) and proliferated in situ as demonstrated by the Fly-FUCCI in vivo cell cycle reporter (Zielke et al., 2014) and immunostaining for a mitotic marker phospho-histone-H3 (pH3) (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D using the Fly-FUCCI reporter and pH3 staining.

claim: The majority of FBAHs are plasmatocytes, interspersed by a smaller number of crystal cells.
source: Staining against the plasmatocyte marker NimrodC1 (NimC1) (Kurucz et al., 2007a) and the crystal cell-specific BcF6:GFP reporter (Tokusumi et al., 2009) showed that like in the sessile tissue (Leitão and Sucena, 2015), the majority of the FBAHs were plasmatocytes, interspersed by a smaller number of crystal cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E using NimC1 and BcF6:GFP markers.

claim: A portion of BcF6:GFP-positive crystal cells also stain for NimC1 and show Hml:DsRed levels similar to plasmatocytes, suggesting they are intermediate hemocytes in the process of plasmatocyte-crystal cell trans-differentiation.
source: Surprisingly, a portion of the BcF6:GFP-positive crystal cells also stained for NimC1 and showed Hml:DsRed levels similar to plasmatocytes, suggesting that these cells are intermediate hemocytes in the process of plasmatocyte-crystal cell trans-differentiation (Figure 2E–E').
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E-E'.

claim: Blackened crystal cells are observed among FBAHs in Hml:DsRed, C7>Atf3WT larvae with the Bc1 mutation.
source: Moreover, we observed blackened crystal cells among FBAHs (Figure 2F) when combining the Hml:DsRed, C7>Atf3WT with the Bc1 mutation (Rizki et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Crystal cell differentiation likely occurs on the adipocyte surface.
source: Since the runaway melanization cascade results in cell death (Lanot et al., 2001; Neyen et al., 2015), we speculate that their differentiation likely occurred on the adipocyte surface.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of melanized crystal cells and knowledge about melanization-induced cell death.

claim: BcF6:GFP expressing and melanized crystal cells are mostly located within FBAH clusters and surrounded by plasmatocytes.
source: Notably, both BcF6:GFP expressing and melanized crystal cells in the Bc1 background were mostly located within the FBAH clusters and were surrounded by plasmatocytes (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: FBAHs detach from the Atf3 overexpressing adipose tissue 48 hours after L. boulardi parasitic infection.
source: We found that the FBAHs detached from the Atf3 overexpressing adipose tissue 48 hr after parasitic infection (Figure 2G–I), and lamellocyte differentiation and capsule formation (Figure 2J, L, N and P) was not impaired to a noticeable extent when compared to control larvae (Figure 2J, K, M and O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Lamellocyte differentiation and capsule formation are not impaired to a noticeable extent in Hml:DsRed, C7>Atf3WT larvae after parasitic infection compared to controls.
source: We found that the FBAHs detached from the Atf3 overexpressing adipose tissue 48 hr after parasitic infection (Figure 2G–I), and lamellocyte differentiation and capsule formation (Figure 2J, L, N and P) was not impaired to a noticeable extent when compared to control larvae (Figure 2J, K, M and O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J-P.

claim: Hemocytes associated with the fat body in C7>Atf3WT larvae display a hematopoietic program reminiscent of sessile blood cells and engage in innate immune defense.
source: Together, these data support the notion that hemocytes associated with the fat body in C7>Atf3WT larvae display a hematopoietic program reminiscent of sessile blood cells and engage in the innate immune defense.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations presented in Figure 2.

claim: Drosophila larval adipocytes are the primary source of basement membrane components for most internal organs, including their own.
source: The Drosophila larval adipocytes are the primary source of the basement membrane components for most internal organs (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011), including their own.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011.

claim: Hindering ECM protein secretion and release can lead to fibrotic accumulation.
source: Hindering ECM protein secretion and release can lead to fibrotic accumulation (Shahab et al., 2015; Zang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shahab et al., 2015 and Zang et al., 2015.

claim: Atf3 has a role in cellular trafficking in epithelial cells.
source: Given the described role of Atf3 in cellular trafficking in epithelial cells (Donohoe et al., 2018), we asked whether the attachment of hemocytes to the Atf3 overexpressing fat body could be caused by changes in the structure or composition of the basement membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Donohoe et al., 2018.

claim: Atf3 overexpression in clonal adipocytes leads to accumulation of Collagen IV, Laminin, and Multiplexin below the basement membrane.
source: Indeed, the visualization of the Vkg::GFP reporter, a fusion protein of Collagen IVα2 and GFP (Morin et al., 2001), as well as immunostaining against Laminin and the Collagen XV/XVIII-type protein Multiplexin (Mp) revealed accumulation of ECM below the basement membrane in Atf3 overexpressing clonal adipocytes (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: C7>Atf3WT fat bodies form deep pericellular folds containing electron-dense material.
source: Transmission-electron microscopy (TEM) further showed that in contrast to the mostly smooth cell membranes of control adipocytes (Figure 3E), the C7>Atf3WT fat bodies formed deep pericellular folds containing electron-dense material (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: ECM proteins are trapped in pericellular spaces in Atf3 overexpressing fat bodies, which might attract hemocytes to the fat body surface.
source: These data suggest that the ECM proteins are trapped in pericellular spaces, which might attract hemocytes to the fat body surface.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of ECM accumulation in pericellular spaces.

claim: Mp knockdown in Atf3 overexpressing adipocytes results in restoration of the stereotypical pattern of sessile hematopoietic pockets at the body wall.
source: Importantly, Mp knockdown in Atf3 overexpressing adipocytes resulted in restoration of the stereotypical pattern of the sessile hematopoietic pockets at the body wall (Figure 3L–O), supporting a notion that upon fat body-specific Atf3 overexpression hemocytes residing in the sessile pockets relocate and expand on the adipose tissue surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L-O.

claim: Upon fat body-specific Atf3 overexpression, hemocytes residing in the sessile pockets relocate and expand on the adipose tissue surface.
source: Importantly, Mp knockdown in Atf3 overexpressing adipocytes resulted in restoration of the stereotypical pattern of the sessile hematopoietic pockets at the body wall (Figure 3L–O), supporting a notion that upon fat body-specific Atf3 overexpression hemocytes residing in the sessile pockets relocate and expand on the adipose tissue surface.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Mp knockdown restores sessile pockets while abolishing FBAHs.

claim: There is a functional link between ECM accumulation and hemocyte attachment to the fat body.
source: These results demonstrate a functional link between ECM accumulation and hemocyte attachment to the fat body, and uncover Mp as a key component of this interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that ECM manipulation affects hemocyte attachment.

claim: Mp is a key component of the interaction between ECM accumulation and hemocyte attachment.
source: These results demonstrate a functional link between ECM accumulation and hemocyte attachment to the fat body, and uncover Mp as a key component of this interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing Mp's necessity for hemocyte attachment.

claim: Loss of Eater completely abolishes sessile hematopoietic pockets, increasing the number of circulating hemocytes.
source: While little is known about the interaction that anchors the hemocytes to the epidermis, a loss of the plasmatocyte-specific phagocytosis receptor Eater (Kocks et al., 2005) was shown to completely abolish sessile pockets, increasing the number of circulating hemocytes (Bretscher et al., 2015; Melcarne et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bretscher et al., 2015 and Melcarne et al., 2019.

claim: C7>Atf3WT larvae homozygous for the eater1 loss of function allele lack both sessile hematopoietic pockets and FBAHs.
source: To address the requirement of Eater in FBAH attachment, we generated C7>Atf3WT larvae homozygous for the eater1 loss of function allele. Strikingly, these larvae lacked both sessile hematopoietic pockets and FBAHs (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-E.

claim: Silencing Eater expression in C7>Atf3WT fat bodies does not interfere with hemocyte-fat body interaction.
source: To validate a specific requirement for Eater in the hemocytes, we first silenced its expression in C7>Atf3WT fat bodies, which did not interfere with hemocyte-fat body interaction (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Simultaneous Atf3 overexpression and Eater knockdown in hemocytes impairs FBAH formation.
source: Next, we generated larvae which aside from C7-GAL4 also carried the HmlΔ-GAL4 hemocyte-specific driver (Sinenko and Mathey-Prevot, 2004). While the expression of Atf3 in both the fat body and the hemocytes did not markedly impact hemocyte adhesion (Figure 4H), simultaneous Atf3 overexpression and Eater knockdown impaired FBAH formation (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I-J.

claim: Eater is a hemocyte-specific adhesion molecule that acts both in the context of sessile pockets and hemocytes on the adipose tissue surface.
source: These data define Eater as a hemocyte-specific adhesion molecule that acts both in the context of the sessile pockets and the hemocytes on the adipose tissue surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing Eater's requirement in both contexts.

claim: Knockdown of Mp in epidermal cells drastically disrupts the pattern of sessile tissue.
source: To this end, we silenced Mp with the a58-GAL4 (larval epidermis), mef2-GAL4 (body wall muscles) and elav-GAL4 (neurons) (Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Lin and Goodman, 1994; Ranganayakulu et al., 1996) drivers to account for the fact that the pockets reside between the larval epidermis and the body wall muscle layer, and their maintenance depends on the activity of peripheral neurons (Makhijani et al., 2011). While loss of Mp in the epidermal cells drastically disrupted the pattern of sessile tissue, resulting in a phenotype strikingly resembling that of eater1 (Figure 4K–O), Mp knockdown in the muscles and the neurons did not result in a similar dispersion of the sessile tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K-O.

claim: Mp knockdown in muscles and neurons does not result in dispersion of sessile tissue.
source: To this end, we silenced Mp with the a58-GAL4 (larval epidermis), mef2-GAL4 (body wall muscles) and elav-GAL4 (neurons) (Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Lin and Goodman, 1994; Ranganayakulu et al., 1996) drivers to account for the fact that the pockets reside between the larval epidermis and the body wall muscle layer, and their maintenance depends on the activity of peripheral neurons (Makhijani et al., 2011). While loss of Mp in the epidermal cells drastically disrupted the pattern of sessile tissue, resulting in a phenotype strikingly resembling that of eater1 (Figure 4K–O), Mp knockdown in the muscles and the neurons did not result in a similar dispersion of the sessile tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Knockdown of Col4a1 and Trol in the epidermis does not mimic the loss of sessile tissue structure caused by Mp knockdown.
source: Interestingly, although effective in suppressing FBAHs on Atf3 overexpressing adipose tissues, knockdown of Col4a1 and Trol in the epidermis did not mimic the loss of sessile tissue structure inflicted by Mp knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Silencing Mp specifically in hemocytes has no visible impact on the integrity of sessile hematopoietic pockets.
source: Furthermore, silencing Mp specifically in hemocytes had no visible impact on the integrity of the sessile hematopoietic pockets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: Eater and Mp are required to facilitate hemocyte-basement membrane interactions both in sessile hematopoietic pockets and the de novo hematopoietic compartment on Atf3 overexpressing fat bodies.
source: These results highlight a requirement for Eater and Mp to facilitate hemocyte-basement membrane interactions both in the case of the naturally occurring sessile hematopoietic pockets and the de novo hematopoietic compartment on Atf3 overexpressing fat bodies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the necessity of both proteins in both contexts.

claim: Drosophila Mp consists of an N-terminal Thrombospondin-like domain, a Collagen triple helix domain, an NC1 trimerization domain, and a C-terminal Endostatin-domain.
source: The Drosophila Mp consists of an N-terminal Thrombospondin-like domain, followed by a Collagen triple helix domain, an NC1 trimerization domain and the C-terminal Endostatin-domain, all of which are present in its mammalian counterparts, Collagens XV and XVIII (Heljasvaara et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heljasvaara et al., 2017.

claim: Mp expression initiates during late embryonic development, mostly in the heart tube and central nervous system, and is needed for motoaxonal pathfinding.
source: Mp expression initiates during late embryonic development, mostly in the heart tube and the central nervous system, and is needed for motoaxonal pathfinding (Harpaz et al., 2013; Meyer and Moussian, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harpaz et al., 2013 and Meyer and Moussian, 2009.

claim: Mp levels markedly increase in the basement membrane of C7>Mp::GFP fat body.
source: Compared to control, Mp levels markedly increased in the basement membrane of C7>Mp::GFP fat body (Figure 5A–B) as determined by immunostaining with a Mp-specific antibody (Harpaz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: GFP signal from Mp::GFP is restricted to the adipocyte cytoplasm, suggesting that the C-terminal end of Mp undergoes proteolytic cleavage.
source: However, GFP signal was restricted to the adipocyte cytoplasm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the C-terminal end of Mp undergoes proteolytic cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that GFP signal is cytoplasmic while Mp staining is in the basement membrane.

claim: Mp::GFP overexpression in the fat body does not induce hemocyte adhesion.
source: Surprisingly, Mp::GFP overexpression in the fat body did not induce hemocyte adhesion (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Mp::GFP overexpression in the fat body leads to complete dispersal of sessile hematopoietic pockets, phenocopying homozygous eater1 mutants.
source: Instead, it led to the complete dispersal of the sessile hematopoietic pockets, phenocopying homozygous eater1 mutants (Figure 5C–E, compare to Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Circulating hemocyte numbers in C7>Mp::GFP larvae significantly increase compared to controls, reaching similar levels as in eater1 mutants.
source: In addition, circulating hemocyte numbers in C7>Mp::GFP larvae significantly increased compared to controls, reaching similar levels as in eater1 mutants (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Mp protein levels increase notably in the circulation of C7>Mp::GFP larvae relative to controls.
source: Immunoblots from the cell free hemolymph revealed a notable increase of the Mp protein in the circulation of C7>Mp::GFP larvae relative to controls (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Fat-body-produced Mp incorporates into the adipocyte ECM and is also released into the hemolymph where it may interfere with hemocyte binding to basement membrane due to a saturation effect.
source: These results indicate that while fat-body-produced Mp incorporates into the adipocyte ECM, it is also released into the hemolymph where it may interact with hemocytes and interfere with their binding to the basement membrane due to a saturation effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Mp overexpression prevents hemocyte attachment despite Mp incorporation into the ECM.

claim: Clonal adipocytes overexpressing Mp::GFP are surrounded by hemocytes that display characteristics of FBAHs.
source: To circumvent the hemolymph overload, we induced Mp::GFP expression only in clones, which resulted in local Mp accumulation over the targeted adipocytes and in their intercellular spaces (Figure 6A–E). Strikingly, clonal adipocytes overexpressing Mp::GFP were surrounded by hemocytes, which displayed previously established characteristics of FBAHs, namely tight clustering and projection of filopodia and lamellipodia, the ability to undergo mitosis on the tissue surface and the presence of crystal cells (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-E.

claim: Mp::GFP expression in the pouch region of the wing disc promotes hemocyte adhesion to this specific domain.
source: Moreover, Mp::GFP expression in the pouch region of the wing disc using the nubbin-Gal4, UAS-mCherry driver (nub>mCherry) promoted hemocyte adhesion to this specific domain (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Hemocyte-epithelial tissue association induced by Mp::GFP expression in wing disc is not provoked by apoptosis of imaginal cells.
source: Of note, this hemocyte epithelial tissue association was not provoked by apoptosis of imaginal cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Mp is not only necessary but also sufficient to facilitate hemocyte attachment to tissue surfaces.
source: Together these results demonstrate that Mp is not only necessary but also sufficient to facilitate hemocyte attachment to tissue surfaces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing both loss-of-function and gain-of-function effects of Mp.

claim: Mp::FLAG co-precipitates with Eater::GFP from Drosophila S2 cell lysates.
source: To this end, we performed co-immunoprecipitation experiments with tagged Eater::GFP and Mp::FLAG proteins in S2 cells, and found that the two proteins indeed co-precipitated (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Mp acts as an interacting partner of Eater on the basement membranes of C7>Atf3WT fat bodies and on the epidermal surface covering sessile hematopoietic pockets.
source: While we cannot exclude that the binding might be indirect, these results present an argument that Mp acts as an interacting partner of Eater on the basement membranes of C7>Atf3WT fat bodies, and on the epidermal surface covering the sessile hematopoietic pockets (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data and functional studies.

claim: Fundamental principles of hematopoiesis and hematopoietic niche formation show similarities across phyla.
source: Fundamental principles of hematopoiesis and hematopoietic niche formation show similarities across phyla (Martinez-Agosto et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martinez-Agosto et al., 2007.

claim: Atf3 overexpression in adipocytes promotes the formation of a de novo hematopoietic compartment on the adipose tissue surface at the expense of the naturally occurring sessile hematopoietic cell pool.
source: We show that Atf3 overexpression in adipocytes promotes the formation of a de novo hematopoietic compartment on the adipose tissue surface at the expense of the naturally occurring sessile hematopoietic cell pool (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: FBAHs show round/spherical morphology and project short filopodia and lamellipodia, which are characteristic of sessile hemocytes.
source: The fat body-associated hemocytes showed round/spherical morphology, and projected short filopodia and lamellipodia, which are characteristic to the sessile hemocytes (Lanot et al., 2001, Figure 2B) and hemocytes adhering to Laminin-coated substrates (Sampson and Williams, 2012), but are distinct from the elongated phenotype of the migratory embryonic macrophages and the pupal hemocytes assisting tissue remodeling (Evans and Wood, 2011; Sampson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The characteristic morphology and absence of tissue debris-phagocytosis and encapsulation response suggest that FBAHs are in a naïve homeostatic state, not engaged in immune response.
source: The characteristic morphology and the absence of tissue debris-phagocytosis and encapsulation response suggest that FBAHs are in a naïve homeostatic state, not engaged in immune response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the morphological and functional observations of FBAHs.

claim: Hemocytes proliferate in the circulation, but the division rate of those in sessile pockets is higher due to stimulating effects of Activin-β secreted by peripheral sensory neurons.
source: Although hemocytes also proliferate in the circulation, the division rate of those in the sessile pockets was shown to be higher due to the stimulating effects of Activin-β secreted by peripheral sensory neurons (Makhijani et al., 2017; Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Makhijani et al., 2017 and Makhijani et al., 2011.

claim: The proliferation of FBAHs may be part of a hemocyte-autonomous developmental program supported by physical adhesion to tissue and cell-cell contacts between attached hemocytes.
source: Since the fat body lacks the innervation of the epidermal cells, the proliferation of FBAHs may be part of a hemocyte-autonomous developmental program, which is supported by the physical adhesion to the tissue and cell-cell contacts between attached hemocytes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that FBAHs proliferate despite lack of neuronal innervation.

claim: Cell-cell contacts are instrumental in the trans-differentiation of plasmatocytes to crystal cells in sessile pockets, which requires Serrate-Notch juxtacrine signaling.
source: Such contacts appear instrumental in the trans-differentiation of plasmatocytes to crystal cells in the sessile pockets, which requires Serrate-Notch juxtacrine signaling among the clustered cells (Leitão and Sucena, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leitão and Sucena, 2015.

claim: Plasmatocyte-crystal cell trans-differentiation in FBAH clusters is cluster-dependent and does not require signals secreted by peripheral neurons.
source: Similarly, FBAH clusters contained fully and partially differentiated crystal cells intermingled with the hemocytes, which suggests that plasmatocyte-crystal cell trans-differentiation is cluster-dependent and does not require signals secreted by peripheral neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of crystal cells in FBAH clusters despite lack of neuronal innervation.

claim: The simultaneous appearance of FBAHs and decline of sessile hemocytes does not significantly impact the amount of circulating blood cells.
source: Importantly, the simultaneous appearance of the FBAHs and a decline of the sessile hemocytes did not significantly impact the amount of circulating blood cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FBAHs are dynamic, entering and leaving the circulation at a comparable rate to sessile hemocytes.
source: This may indicate that FBAHs are dynamic, entering and leaving the circulation at a comparable rate to sessile hemocytes (Honti et al., 2010; Makhijani et al., 2011; Welman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that circulating hemocyte numbers remain stable despite FBAH formation, supported by citations.

claim: Knockdown of Col4a1 and Trol strongly suppresses fat body association of hemocytes in Atf3 overexpressing fat bodies.
source: In contrast, the knockdown of Col4a1 (Collagen IVα1) and Trol (Perlecan) strongly suppressed fat body association of hemocytes, while silencing Vkg partially inhibited blood cell attachment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–1E and 1I) and silencing of Laminin-A, -B1 and -B2 (LanA, LanB1, LanB2) had no effect on the presence of FBAHs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-E and 1I.

claim: Silencing Vkg partially inhibits blood cell attachment to Atf3 overexpressing fat bodies.
source: In contrast, the knockdown of Col4a1 (Collagen IVα1) and Trol (Perlecan) strongly suppressed fat body association of hemocytes, while silencing Vkg partially inhibited blood cell attachment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–1E and 1I) and silencing of Laminin-A, -B1 and -B2 (LanA, LanB1, LanB2) had no effect on the presence of FBAHs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-E and 1I.

claim: Silencing of Laminin-A, -B1 and -B2 has no effect on the presence of FBAHs.
source: In contrast, the knockdown of Col4a1 (Collagen IVα1) and Trol (Perlecan) strongly suppressed fat body association of hemocytes, while silencing Vkg partially inhibited blood cell attachment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–1E and 1I) and silencing of Laminin-A, -B1 and -B2 (LanA, LanB1, LanB2) had no effect on the presence of FBAHs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-I.

claim: Inhibition of Col4a1 and Trol causes marked alterations to fat body structure and impacts animal viability.
source: It is important to note that similar to SPARC silencing, inhibition of Col4a1 and Trol caused marked alterations to fat body structure and impacted animal viability, as reported previously (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011; Shahab et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011 and Shahab et al., 2015.

claim: Mp downregulation completely abolishes hemocyte association to Atf3 overexpressing fat body without adverse effect on tissue integrity.
source: Surprisingly, downregulation of Mp manifested by a noticeable reduction of Mp levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–2B), completely abolished hemocyte association to the Atf3 overexpressing fat body (Figure 3G-K and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) without any adverse effect on tissue integrity, although the pericellular membrane folds with ECM material were still present (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-K and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pericellular membrane folds with ECM material are still present after Mp knockdown in Atf3 overexpressing fat bodies.
source: Surprisingly, downregulation of Mp manifested by a noticeable reduction of Mp levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–2B), completely abolished hemocyte association to the Atf3 overexpressing fat body (Figure 3G-K and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) without any adverse effect on tissue integrity, although the pericellular membrane folds with ECM material were still present (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Not the membrane folds, but their specific content is responsible for FBAH adhesion.
source: These results indicate that not the membrane folds, but their specific content is responsible for FBAH adhesion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that membrane folds persist after Mp knockdown but hemocytes do not attach.

claim: Mp knockdown combined with SPARC silencing significantly decreases FBAH amounts compared to SPARC silencing alone, despite disrupted fat body structure.
source: To confirm this notion, we combined Mp knockdown with silencing of SPARC, which we found to exacerbate pericellular ECM accumulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–2H). While the structure of C7>Atf3WTSPARCRNAiMpRNAi fat body remained disrupted and blebbing was still present (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G) the amount of FBAHs was significantly decreased compared to C7>Atf3WTSPARCRNAi adipose tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F-H.

claim: Niche alterations can drive premature hematopoietic aging and malignancies.
source: In contrast, emerging evidence suggest that niche alterations can drive premature hematopoietic aging and malignancies (Ho et al., 2019; Walkley et al., 2007a; Walkley et al., 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2019, Walkley et al., 2007a, and Walkley et al., 2007b.

claim: Mp-containing basement membranes may have specific functions in cell adhesion and migration distinct from ubiquitous Col4a1 and Vkg.
source: Mp expression initiates during late embryonic development, mostly in the heart tube and the central nervous system, and is needed for motoaxonal pathfinding (Harpaz et al., 2013; Meyer and Moussian, 2009). These traits are distinct from the ubiquitous Col4a1 and Vkg, suggesting that Mp-containing basement membranes may have specific functions in cell adhesion and migration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the distinct expression pattern and function of Mp compared to other ECM components.

claim: Increased Mp levels in the hemolymph compete with basement membrane-incorporated Mp for binding to its receptor on hemocytes, preventing their association with epidermal or fat body ECMs.
source: We propose that the increased Mp levels in the hemolymph compete with the basement membrane-incorporated protein for the binding of its receptor on the hemocytes preventing their association with the epidermal or fat body ECMs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the observation that whole fat body Mp overexpression prevents hemocyte attachment.

claim: Both tissue specificity and levels of endogenous Mp expression are tightly regulated.
source: These results also suggest that both the tissue specificity and the levels of endogenous Mp expression are tightly regulated.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Mp overexpression has different effects depending on whether it is whole-tissue or clonal.

claim: Low amounts of Mp in the epidermal basement membrane are sufficient to anchor hemocytes through a specific and strong interaction between Mp and its receptor on hemocytes.
source: In the context of the sessile hematopoietic pockets, this could mean that low amounts of Mp in the epidermal basement membrane are sufficient to anchor hemocytes through a specific and strong interaction between Mp and its receptor on the hemocytes.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of hemocyte anchoring in sessile pockets.

claim: The mammalian counterpart of Mp, Collagen XV, is restricted to cardiac and skeletal muscles.
source: Interestingly, the mammalian counterpart of Mp, Collagen XV is restricted to the cardiac and skeletal muscles (Hägg et al., 1997) while its other ortholog Collagen XVIII is ubiquitously expressed throughout development (Miosge et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hägg et al., 1997.

claim: Collagen XVIII is ubiquitously expressed throughout development.
source: Interestingly, the mammalian counterpart of Mp, Collagen XV is restricted to the cardiac and skeletal muscles (Hägg et al., 1997) while its other ortholog Collagen XVIII is ubiquitously expressed throughout development (Miosge et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miosge et al., 2003.

claim: Both ColXV and ColXVIII undergo posttranslational modifications including addition of chondroitin- or heparan-sulfate side-chains.
source: Both ColXV and ColXVIII undergo a multitude of posttranslational modifications, which include the addition of chondroitin- or heparan-sulfate side-chains (Dong et al., 2003), and extensive protein cleavage which produces Endostatin, an anti-angiogenic peptide that is widely studied because of its link to cell migration, proliferation and tumorigenesis (O'Reilly et al., 1997; Walia et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2003.

claim: Extensive protein cleavage of ColXV and ColXVIII produces Endostatin, an anti-angiogenic peptide linked to cell migration, proliferation and tumorigenesis.
source: Both ColXV and ColXVIII undergo a multitude of posttranslational modifications, which include the addition of chondroitin- or heparan-sulfate side-chains (Dong et al., 2003), and extensive protein cleavage which produces Endostatin, an anti-angiogenic peptide that is widely studied because of its link to cell migration, proliferation and tumorigenesis (O'Reilly et al., 1997; Walia et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Reilly et al., 1997 and Walia et al., 2015.

claim: Mp is modified by Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chains.
source: Similarly, Mp was found to be modified by Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chains, and the overexpression of its N- and C-terminal domains had distinct effects on the motoaxon guidance (Meyer and Moussian, 2009; Momota et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meyer and Moussian, 2009 and Momota et al., 2011.

claim: Overexpression of Mp's N- and C-terminal domains has distinct effects on motoaxon guidance.
source: Similarly, Mp was found to be modified by Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chains, and the overexpression of its N- and C-terminal domains had distinct effects on the motoaxon guidance (Meyer and Moussian, 2009; Momota et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meyer and Moussian, 2009 and Momota et al., 2011.

claim: Eater is a member of the Nimrod superfamily of transmembrane phagocytosis receptors that contain multiple EGF-like domains.
source: The hemocyte-specific counterpart of Mp, Eater, on the other hand, is a member of the Nimrod superfamily of transmembrane phagocytosis receptors that contain multiple EGF-like domains (Kocks et al., 2005; Somogyi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kocks et al., 2005 and Somogyi et al., 2008.

claim: Nimrod family members have no direct orthologs in mammals.
source: While Nimrod family members have no direct orthologs in mammals, multiple EGF-like domain-containing transmembrane proteins such as MEGF10 have been associated with cell adhesion and migration (Suzuki and Nakayama, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki and Nakayama, 2007.

claim: Multiple EGF-like domain-containing transmembrane proteins such as MEGF10 have been associated with cell adhesion and migration in mammals.
source: While Nimrod family members have no direct orthologs in mammals, multiple EGF-like domain-containing transmembrane proteins such as MEGF10 have been associated with cell adhesion and migration (Suzuki and Nakayama, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki and Nakayama, 2007.

claim: Mp's interaction with Eater may be due to particular posttranslational modifications such as chondroitin sulfate addition or proteolytic cleavage.
source: Since Mp is extensively processed upon its secretion to the extracellular space, it is tempting to speculate that its interaction with Eater may be due to particular posttranslational modifications, such as chondroitin sulfate addition or proteolytic cleavage (Meyer and Moussian, 2009; Momota et al., 2011), which sets it apart from the ubiquitously present ECM proteins in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of Mp-Eater interaction based on known posttranslational modifications of Mp.
